message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This evaluation gives the University the evidence it has been asking for on continuation. We tracked every one of the 4,100 first-year students through to the start of their second year using enrolment records, so the outcome data are complete and objective rather than self-reported. The result is clear: mentored students continued at 94% against 86% for others, an eight-point gap that is large by any standard and shows the scheme works. The financial case follows directly. Those 99 or so additional continuing students are worth around £1.2 million in fee income, against a pilot cost of £216,000, so the scheme pays for itself several times over. The qualitative feedback, with a 4.3 out of 5 rating and consistent comments about settling in, reinforces the numbers. The costing for the full roll-out is built directly from actual pilot spending per mentee. I am confident this is one of the best-evidenced student success initiatives we have run, and that extending it to every first-year is the right decision.
</author>

<document>
Evaluation of the First-Year Peer Mentoring Scheme, 2025-26
Student Success Unit, Northbridge University, July 2026

1. Purpose
Continuation from first to second year is a key regulatory and financial measure for the University. In 2024-25, 13% of full-time first-year undergraduates did not continue into their second year. In 2025-26 the University piloted a peer mentoring scheme for first-year students. This report evaluates the pilot and recommends whether it should be extended.

2. The scheme
Students in their second or third year were recruited and trained as mentors, and each was matched with up to eight first-year mentees from the same faculty. Mentors held a group session every fortnight during the first term and were available for one-to-one meetings throughout the year. Mentors were paid £1,200 for the year. They attended a half-day training session in September covering listening skills, signposting to support services and safeguarding, and were supported by a coordinator in each faculty. First-year students were invited to opt in during welcome week.

Recruiting mentors proved harder than expected. We advertised 200 mentor posts and filled 155, which allowed us to offer places to 1,240 first-year students (155 mentors with eight mentees each). Mentee places were taken up within the first two weeks and a waiting list was closed at 300 names.

3. Who took part
Of the 4,100 full-time first-year students, 1,240 took part. Mentees were more likely than other first-years to be living in university halls (78% compared with 52%) and were somewhat more likely to have entered with higher tariff qualifications. They were similar to non-mentees in age and gender.

4. Results
Table 1. Continuation into second year, 2025-26 entrants
Group | Students | Continuing to year two | Continuation rate
Mentored | 1,240 | 1,166 | 94.0%
Not mentored | 2,860 | 2,460 | 86.0%
All first-years | 4,100 | 3,626 | 88.4%

Mentored students were eight percentage points more likely to continue into their second year. Overall continuation rose to 88.4%, from 87% the previous year.

The eight-point gap is clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation. Applied to the 1,240 mentees, it means that around 99 students continued who would otherwise have left. At £9,250 a year in tuition fee income, these students are worth about £1.2 million to the University in their second year alone.

Mentees rated the scheme 4.3 out of 5 in the end-of-year survey, and many commented that it helped them settle in and find out about support services. Mentors reported that the role improved their own confidence and employability.

5. Costs
The pilot cost £186,000 for mentor pay, £12,000 for training and £18,000 for coordination, a total of £216,000, or about £174 per mentee.

6. Recommendation
We recommend that from 2026-27 peer mentoring becomes a standard part of the first-year experience, with every full-time first-year student allocated a mentor automatically rather than opting in. On the pilot's costs of about £174 per mentee, this would cost around £714,000 a year for 4,100 students. On the pilot's results, it would raise continuation to around 94% across the whole first-year cohort, a gain of over 200 continuing students a year, and the fee income retained would cover the cost several times over.

7. Conclusion
The pilot has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points, pays for itself many times over, and is valued by mentees and mentors alike. Extending it to all first-year students is a clear opportunity to improve outcomes and secure the University's continuation performance.
</document>
response:
# Review: First-Year Peer Mentoring Evaluation

The scheme may well work, and the outcome data are a real strength. But the report does not yet show that mentoring *caused* the eight-point gap. Several figures in the financial case are wrong or don't follow, and the roll-out plan assumes something the pilot showed is hard to do. I'd revise before this goes to decision-makers.

## 1. The eight-point gap is not evidence of impact (the main issue)

Complete enrolment records tell you *what happened* to every student. They tell you nothing about *why*. The comparison problem is visible in the report itself:

- **Students opted in.** Students who sign up in welcome week, and fill every place within two weeks, are likely more engaged and organised. Those traits predict continuation regardless of mentoring.
- **Section 3 shows the groups differ on known predictors.** Mentees were much more likely to live in halls (78% vs 52%) and somewhat more likely to have higher-tariff entry. Both are associated with higher continuation.

So some, possibly most, of the eight points may reflect *who joined* rather than *what the scheme did*. "Clear evidence that peer mentoring improves continuation" (Section 4) and "has shown that peer mentoring improves continuation by eight percentage points" (Section 7) are not supported as written. "Large by any standard" in your summary also needs dropping or qualifying.

**What you can do with existing data:**
- **Use the 300-name waiting list.** These students wanted mentoring but didn't get it, so they're a much fairer comparison than all non-mentees. Report their continuation rate alongside the mentees'. This is probably the single most valuable addition.
- **Compare like with like.** Show continuation for mentees vs non-mentees *within* halls/non-halls and tariff bands, or fit a simple adjusted model. If a gap survives, that's far more persuasive.
- **Check engagement.** If mentees who attended more sessions continued at higher rates, that supports the case (though it's not conclusive on its own).

**A sanity check that points the same way:** if mentoring had added 99 continuing students, overall continuation would have risen about 2.4 points (99 ÷ 4,100). It actually rose 1.4 points (87% to 88.4%), about 57 students. Year-on-year comparisons are noisy, so this isn't proof. But it's consistent with the true effect being smaller than eight points.

## 2. Errors in the financial case

| Claim | Check | Issue |
|---|---|---|
| 99 students × £9,250 = "about £1.2 million" | 99 × £9,250 = **£915,750** | Overstated by ~£280k. £1.2m would need ~130 students. |
| Pilot cost £216,000 | 186 + 12 + 18 = 216 ✓; 155 × £1,200 = £186,000 ✓ | Correct |
| £174 per mentee | 216,000 ÷ 1,240 = £174.19 ✓ | Correct |
| Roll-out £714,000 | £174 × 4,100 ≈ £713,400 ✓ | Arithmetic fine, but see Section 3 |
| Table 1 rates and totals | All check out ✓ | Correct |

Beyond the arithmetic:
- **The £0.92m depends entirely on the 99 being caused by mentoring.** If half the gap is selection, the return halves. If most of it is, the return largely disappears. "Pays for itself many times over" should be presented as conditional, ideally with a range.
- **£9,250 is home undergraduate fee revenue, not net gain.** Fine as a headline, but say so, and note that fee levels vary by student.

## 3. The roll-out plan has a feasibility gap

- **Mentor numbers.** At eight mentees per mentor, 4,100 students need about **513 mentors**. The pilot advertised 200 posts and filled only 155. The report needs a recruitment plan (higher pay? larger groups? broader eligibility?). Any of those changes the cost per mentee, so "built directly from actual pilot spending" won't hold.
- **Fixed vs variable costs.** Coordination and training may not scale linearly. Check whether £18,000 of faculty coordination stretches to over three times the mentors.
- **Moving from opt-in to automatic allocation changes the population.** The students now being added are the ones who *didn't* volunteer. They have lower baseline continuation and are likely to engage less. Assuming they'd reach 94% is the weakest claim in the report. The "over 200 extra continuing students" figure inherits this problem.

## 4. Smaller points

- **Satisfaction survey:** give the response rate. Satisfied mentees are more likely to respond, and a 4.3/5 rating shows the scheme is valued, not that it improves continuation. Keep it as supporting evidence only.
- **Mentor benefits:** worth keeping, but they rest on self-report.
- **Section 1 vs Section 4:** "13% did not continue" and "87%" are consistent, but use one form throughout.

## 5. Suggested reframing of the recommendation

Rather than full automatic roll-out on current evidence, consider:
1. Add the waiting-list and adjusted comparisons to this report. If they still show a solid gap, the case is much stronger.
2. **Expand in 2026-27 in a way that generates evidence.** For example, phase it in by faculty, or randomly allocate places if demand again exceeds supply. Since you're capacity-limited anyway, a lottery costs nothing extra and would give a clean answer within a year.
3. Cost the roll-out from a realistic mentor recruitment plan rather than scaling the pilot's per-mentee figure.

This would let you say "the scheme is popular, the early signs are promising, and here is how we'll confirm the effect as we scale." That's a position the University can defend if continuation doesn't jump to 94%.
